Put variables declarations at the beginning of each block

From Source to Runtime

C Header files (.h) — elegant solution for:

organizing code on many files
reusing code, even in form of compiled library

On build-time, only headers are used
On link-time and runtime, only libraries are needed and used (no headers)

Build command needs:
Build time

Link time

switches for linking configuration

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Building your code
Typical compilation command:
clang [options] -Ipath/to/includes -Lpath/to/libs -llibrary_name \
  -o output_file source1.c source2.c source3.c

Most common compilers are gcc and clang (we’ll use clang)
The [options] list and the list of source files can be long and tedious to type

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Building assistants: IDE or CLI

GNU Make: command-line program for building complex projects via special scripts called Makefiles. A Makefile is typically complex to write and maintain
CMake: command-line program that takes a configuration file (CMakeLists.txt) and generates a temporary building environment (typically using GNU Make). Easier to write and maintain than Makefile

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
CMake Script


Steps:

project setup
define common switches
define headers and library locations
define targets
define install behavior



cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.9)
set(CMAKE_C_COMPILER "clang")
# Set project name, version, and language
project(C-CNC VERSION 0.0.1 LANGUAGES C)
# Set common compile options and preprocessor definitions
add_compile_options(-std=gnu11 -fPIC)
add_definitions(-D_GNU_SOURCE)
# Define the list of source files
set(SOURCE_DIR ${CMAKE_HOME_DIRECTORY}/src) #set a variable
file(GLOB LIB_SOURCES "${SOURCE_DIR}/*.c") #put into LIB_SOURCES the globbed list
# Parametrically create some file from template
configure_file(
  ${SOURCE_DIR}/version.h.in
  ${SOURCE_DIR}/version.h
)
# define header directories
include_directories(
  ${CMAKE_HOME_DIRECTORY}/machine/src
)

# Define TARGETS, i.e. output objects
# Library target:
add_library(ccnclib STATIC ${LIB_SOURCES})
target_link_libraries(ccnclib machine)
# Main executable
add_executable(ccnc ${SOURCE_DIR}/main/ccnc.c)
add_dependencies(ccnc ccnclib)
target_link_libraries(ccnc ccnclib)

# INSTALL
set(CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX ${CMAKE_HOME_DIRECTORY})
install(TARGETS ccnclib ccnc
  RUNTIME DESTINATION bin
  LIBRARY DESTINATION lib
  ARCHIVE DESTINATION lib
)

CMake
Building with cmake takes 2+1 steps:

Configuration: cmake -Bbuild_dir

Installing: cmake --build build_dir -t install

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Programming C as a Pro
Problem 1:

complex programs are made of many functions that have to pass around data. C function arguments are passed by value (i.e. copied!)
for good performance you need to minimize info passed by functions

Solution: learn to use pointers

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Programming C as a Pro
Problem 2:

C function can only return a single value
C functions cannot return compound types (arrays!)

Solution: learn to use pointers

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Programming C as a Pro
Problem 3:

complex programs are made of many functions
they also depend on external libraries
the code must be readable and understandable

Solution: carefully distribute code in different files, and use flexible build software

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Stack vs. Heap memory







FIFO access (fast)
Typ. ~8 Mb capacity per thread (check with command ulimit -s)






Random access (slower)
Virtually unlimited

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Tricky Pointers

Standard variables are defined on the stack memory
You get the pointer to variable var with &var
You get the value of pointer var_p with *var_p
Arrays are pointers to their first element, but stack arrays have a limited maximum size (system dependent)
Variables on stack are eliminated from memory on exiting from local scope

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Tricky Pointers

Pointers requiring large (or dynamic) memory can be defined on the heap memory
You allocate a pointer on the heap with the malloc() family of functions
malloc’d variables are not freed upon exiting from local scope
For every malloc() you need one free(), or you have a memory leak ☠️☠️☠️

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
section: Ways for returning an array in C
text:
Ways for returning an array in C

Use malloc() in the caller and pass the pointer as an inout argument (easier)
Call malloc() inside the function and return that pointer (easy, but you cannot return anything else, like error status)
Pass a double pointer to the callee as an inout argument, use malloc() inside the function (not so easy, but you can also return a status value)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Memory leaks

There must be exactly one free() for every malloc()
Sometimes the malloc() is implicit, e.g. asprintf() and similar functions (those that take double pointers for allocating and returning an array!)
Leaked memory is restored on process exit
BUT, long running processes MUST avoid memory leaks, especially when the leak occurs within loops

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT protocol

MQTT stands for Message Queue Telemetry Transport
Actually, there is no queue but rather a publish-subscribe architecture
The protocol is lightweight: it minimizes the overhead of messages
It is about 100 times faster than REST HTTP messaging (in terms of maximum msg/s)
It is not the fastest protocol (ZeroMQ is faster), but it is simple to implement and well balanced

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT protocol

In MQTT there are 3 different roles: publisher, subscriber, broker

The publisher is the information producer (to be implemented)
The subscriber is the information consumer (to be implemented)
The broker is a server that relays publisher messages to (possibly many) subscribers (already available)

Messages are published under topics
Topics are arranged hierarchically: ccnc/x/pos, ccnc/y/vel

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT protocol
Subscribers can subscribe to more than one topic, possibly also using wildcards (+ or #):

ccnc/+/pos means any single word in between ccnc and pos (as ccnc/x/pos and ccnc/y/pos, but not ccnc/x/nominal/pos)
ccnc/#/pos means anything (including multiple branches) under ccnc and ending with /pos

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT protocol

Publishers can publish messages to many different topics, but one at a time (no wildcards!)
A message is also called a payload: any sequence of bytes, up to a maximum 268435456 bytes (\(2^{28}\), ~260 Mb)
Bigger payloads need to be split (or compressed)
Messages are assigned with a quality of service level (QoS) and with an optional retain flag

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT protocol
The QoS level states the reliability of a message:

QoS 0: a message is delivered at most once
QoS 1: a message is delivered at least once
QoS 2: a message is delivered exactly once

QoS 0 is “fire-and-forget”: less reliable but with minimum information exchange. QoS 2 has a delivery confirmation: 100% reliable, but slower

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT protocol

The retain flag, when set, instructs the broker to deliver the message to any subscriber connecting in the future

It is a kind of “last known value” clause

There are also last will and testament (LWT) messages: these are messages delivered as soon as the broker detects that the client has disconnected
Note: the roles of publisher and subscriber are semantic: any given process can simultaneously act as publisher and subscriber, if needed. Both are clients of the broker server

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT Applications

There are many available broker services, like mosquitto, Paho, HiveMQ, Mosca, EMQ X, VerneMQ.
As well, there are many libraries for implementing MQTT clients (pub+sub) in virtually any known programming language
We will refer to mosquitto (the broker) and libmosquitto (the C library)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT Broker
The mosquitto broker can be installed as a linux service, but it is much quicker and easier to use a docker container:
docker run -d --rm \
  --name mosquitto \
  -p 1883:1883 \
  -v "${PWD}/mosquitto.conf:/mosquitto/config/mosquitto.conf" \
  eclipse-mosquitto

-d --rm: as daemon, remove on exit
--name mosquitto: give it a name
-p 1883:1883: expose port 1883
-v ...: config file
eclipse-mosquitto: name of the image

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT Broker
The mosquitto config file (mosquitto.conf) typically contains at minimum:
allow_anonymous true
listener 1883
protocol mqtt
This accepts any connection. In production, you might want to require passwords and encrypted connections.

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

Documentation is on https://mosquitto.org/api
The library namespace is mosqpp, the main class is mosquittopp
Typical sequence of operation:

Start > library init > client init > client connect > set callbacks > loop { publish messages & update sockets } > free resources > stop

Callbacks are methods automatically called on given events (e.g. successful connection, receiving subscribed message, …)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

Library init: mosqpp::lib_init()

It simply MUST be called before any other mosquitto call

Library cleanup: mosqpp::lib_cleanup() (in destructor)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

Client init: auto mqt = mosquittopp(id, clean)

id: can be a name (useful for debugging, only visible to the broker)
clean: ask the broker to delete all messages and subscriptions on disconnect

Typically, you derive a class from mosquittopp

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

Client connect: mosquittopp::connect(broker_addr, broker_port, keepalive)

Connect the object to a given broker host and port
The broker pings the client (if no messages arrive) every keepalive seconds to verify if it is connected

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

Implement callbacks: mosquittopp::on_message(const struct mosquitto_message *message) (et similia)

Object calls on_message each time a message is received

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library
All network operations are just scheduled by subscribe and publish functions. They are actually performed in two alternative ways:

By repeatedly/cyclically calling mosquittopp::loop() (preferred if you already have a loop)
By starting a parallel thread that iteratively calls mosquittopp::loop(): this is done by calling mosquittopp::loop_start() just after mosquittopp::connect()

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

To schedule the publishing of a message, use mosquittopp::publish(mid, topic, len, payload, qos, retain)

The payload is any sequence of len bytes (a string or a binary object)
The message ID mid is typically NULL

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library

When a message is received, the on_message callback is executed
It gets the message as a struct mosquitto_message, which contains:

Message ID (if any), topic, payload, payload length, QoS level, retain flag.

It does not contain any info on the publisher!
The subscriber HAS NO WAY for identifying the publisher (unless it is written in the payload or topic)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
MQTT library
When done, you should, in this order:

Unsubscribe all subscriptions
Call mosquittopp::loop or mosquittopp::loop_stop
Disconnect from broker
Call mosqpp::lib_cleanup

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Cargo cult in anthropology



A cargo cult is a belief system, in which adherents perform rituals which they believe will cause a more technologically advanced society to deliver goods
Many examples in remote Pacific islands, where inhabitants replicate US army “rituals” in the hope of calling a cargo delivery

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Cargo Cult programming/engineering
Typical pattern:

You don’t know how to solve a problem
You type “How to do something in my language?” in Google (or ChatGPT!)
You end up on Stackoverflow (or similar sites) or get an AI-generated code
You copy and paste the first solution, which you cannot fully understand but it seems to work

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
section: Why is that a bad habit?
text:
Why is that a bad habit?

At best, it messes up your coding style (e.g. using variableNames rather than variable_names)
You may look amateur and naïve to those who read your code (among them, your prospective employer!)
Foremost, you are losing control on your code, which may work fine in the stackoverflow/AI example, but much probably does hidden nasty things once embedded in your code
Additionally, your problem understanding does not improve

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
section: Doesn’t happen only when you code
text:
Doesn’t happen only when you code

There are many examples of cargo cult engineering as well
Each time you accept an existing solution just because it works in another emplacement, and without fully understanding it, you are a cargo cultist
Always question any solution; ask why; do not accept any solution that you cannot fully understand, at least in its outer structure (input/output relations, interfaces, specifications)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Tool radius compensation

G-code standard supports a feature for offsetting the tool trajectory to the left or to the right of the trajectory by an amount equal to the tool radius
This is only affecting the X-Y projection of the trajectory, Z values remain unchanged
The TRC is set to the left with G41, to the right with G42 and is disabled with G40
TRC is fully active at the end of the current block

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Tool radius compensation



TRC offsets the tool center path (programmed points) according to G41/G42
New target points are calculated for each block on the basis of the offset intersection with the next block (arc or line)
Disabled for rapid motions

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Line-Line case


We need to calculate the point \(D\):

Given the line equation \(y = ax + b\), we need to calculate the equation of the offset line(s)
Calculate \(D\) as intercept between the two offset lines

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Line-Line case



Given \(y = ax + b\), the equation of the offset line is \(y = ax + b - v\)
Being \(a = u/r\), it follows that: \(v = \sqrt{u^2 + r^2} = r\sqrt{a^2 + 1}\)
So, \(y = ax + b \pm r\sqrt{a^2 + 1}\)
The sign depends on G41/G42 and on the path direction

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Line-Line case


Intersection \(D\) between
\(y = a_1 x + b_1 - v_1 = a_1 x + b_{o,1}\)
and
\(y = a_2 x + b_2 - v_2 = a_2 x + b_{o,2}\)
has coordinates:
\[(x_i, y_i) = \left(\frac{b_{o,2} - b_{o,1}}{a_1 - a_2}, \frac{b_{o,1}a_2 - b_{o,2}a_1}{a_2 - a_1}\right)\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Line-Line case



Exception: when two segments are collinear (\(a = a_1 = a_2\)), the intercept is undefined
The new intersection node is set at an offset \(r\) perpendicular to the segments

\[C = \begin{cases} (0, -r), & \text{when } a = 0 \\ r(s, -s/a) \text{ with } s = \frac{a}{|a|}\sqrt{\frac{a^2}{1 + a^2}}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
Interactive example on https://www.geogebra.org/m/pmdtaprr

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 2
text:
Line-Arc (or Arc-Line) case


Similar to line-line case, but with a caveat:

Line-circle intersection gives two points, \(G\) and \(B_r\): you have to select the intersection that is closer to the node to be offset (\(B\) in figure)

Digital Manufacturing

title: Course Introduction
text:
Digital Manufacturing

Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT): has to support communications among CPSs (M2M communication)
IP protocol: IPv4 has \(2^{32} \simeq 4.3 \times 10^9\) addresses, IPv6 has \(2^{128} \simeq 3.4 \times 10^{39}\) addresses. IPv6 adoption is slow because of NAT and its rescue for IPv4 addresses exhaustion problem

title: Course Introduction
text:
OSI Networking Model

Networking stack: according to the Internet model, networking happens over a stack of 4 layers




Link layer (L0): physical carrier (Ethernet Cable, WiFi, etc) and its protocol (MAC, 802.11, ARP, etc)
Internet (or network) layer (L1): IPv4, IPv6, ICMP
Transport layer (L2): TCP, UDP
Application layer (L3): HTTP, FTP, IMAP, LDAP, …





OSI layers

title: Course Introduction
text:
Digital Manufacturing

Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT): has to support communications among CPSs (M2M communication)
Level 0 protocols: 5G (low latency!)
IP protocol (L1): beside address space, IPv6 has other advantages (complex multicasting, autoconfiguration, IPsec). Its adoption is still slow, though
Level 3 protocols: from REST (HTTPS) to lightweight protocols (MQTT, ZeroMQ, AMQP, OPC-UA)

title: Course Introduction

REST vs Message Queuing



REpresentational State Transfer: IoT extension of HTTP

Verbose (large overhead)
Complex (PUT/GET/POST/DELETE)
Polling-based
Point-to-point (n clients to 1 server)

title: Course Introduction
text:
HTTP overhead


Request phrase: GET / HTTP/1.1 (14 × 2 bytes)
The HTTP frame takes 153 bytes total
The full request stack takes 437 bytes




Wireshark capture

title: Course Introduction
text:
HTTP overhead


Response phrase: 77 bytes + HTML
The whole HTTP frame takes 937 bytes (including 819 bytes of HTML)
The full response stack takes 1201 bytes, 382 bytes for a blank page




Wireshark capture

title: Course Introduction
text:
How to reduce overhead

Simpler transport layer (L2) protocol: UDP has no SYN/ACK/FIN frames (but no confirmation of delivery!)

AND/OR

Simpler application layer (L3) protocols, where the data frame is as naked as possible
Trade reliability and robustness for bandwidth and latency

title: Course Introduction
text:
How to reduce overhead

Reliability and robustness are very important for IoP communications: variety of web servers, web browsers and document formats, and the web must “just work”
They are also important in IoT (things must do their tasks) but we can enforce standards and minimize possible sources of unexpected conditions

title: Course Introduction

IoT messages are typically smaller but much more frequent than IoP messages, and may need to follow routes more complex than n-to-1 (clients–server)

Need to minimize overhead
Need to support flexible topologies

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Manufacturing systems

To give shape to a block of raw material (workpiece) there are three possibilities:

Deform it: forming processes (motion axes: 1+)
Cut it: material removal (or subtractive) processes (motion axes: 2.5+)
Build on it: additive manufacturing processes (motion axes: 2.5+)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Manufacturing systems


We skip over forming processes, where motion planning and control is trivial (with exceptions!)
In subtractive and additive manufacturing there is a tool performing the process (a mill, a polarized wire, an extruding nozzle, …), whose motion is performed by synchronized action of two or more axes, typically in cartesian arrangement
The motion (trajectory and speed) must be planned according to geometry and process specifics

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Reference case: Turning/Milling

The majority of products involve machining, either directly, or indirectly (dies are machined)
Machining involves a combination of linear and rotary motions:

In turning, the workpiece is rotating, the tool is displacing
In drilling and milling the tool is rotating and there is a combined relative displacement between tool and workpiece








Important


Regardless the process, understanding its physics and the governing parameters is essential to design the manufacturing system and its control algorithms

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Machining parameters

Mechanism of chip formation depends

on the relative speed of tool and workpiece (cutting speed)
on the cross section of removed material

Cutting speed and cross section (tool parameters) depend in turn on trajectory, rotary and translation speeds (machining parameters)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Turning
Machining parameters to be calculated are spindle speed, feed rate, and spindle power:


\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Rotational speed:}\quad & N = \frac{v}{\pi D_0} \\
\text{Diameter:}\quad & D_f = D_0 - 2d \\
\text{Feed rate:}\quad & f = N f_r \\
\text{Machining time:}\quad & T_m = \frac{L}{f} = \frac{\pi D_0 L}{f_r v} \\
\text{Material Removal Rate:}\quad & MRR = v f_r d
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Drilling
Machining parameters to be calculated are spindle speed, feed rate, and spindle power:


\[
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{v}{\pi D} \\
f &= N f_r \\
T_m &= \frac{t + A}{f} \\
A &= \frac{D}{2}\tan\left(\frac{\pi - \theta}{2}\right) \\
MRR &= \frac{\pi D^2 f}{4}
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Example
We have to set up a milling process on Aluminum, which has \(p_s = 12.56\) W min/cm³
The tool manufacturer suggests \(v = 1000\) m/min and \(f_z = 0.1\) mm/tooth
The mill has a diameter of \(30\) mm and does face milling with full overlapping, has \(3\) teeth and removes a layer of \(2\) mm
\[
\begin{aligned}
N &= \frac{v}{\pi D} = \frac{1000\ \text{m/min}}{\pi\, 30\ \text{mm}} = 10610\ \text{rpm} \\
f &= f_z z N = 0.1\ \text{mm} \cdot 3 \cdot 10610\ \text{rpm} = 3183\ \text{mm/min} \\
MRR &= w d f = 30\ \text{mm} \cdot 2\ \text{mm} \cdot 3183\ \text{mm/min} = 190980\ \text{mm}^3/\text{min} \\
P &= MRR\, p_s = 190.98\ \text{cm}^3/\text{min} \cdot 12.56\ \text{W min/cm}^3 \simeq 2.4\ \text{kW}
\end{aligned}
\]






Note


The machininst must always ensure that the required maximum power does not exceet that available at the spindle. If not, some of the machining parameters must be reduced (usually \(d\) and or \(w\))

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Cutting Economics
The cost of machining depends on:

labor: hourly cost of trained personnel
machinery: purchase cost / machine life
raw material: cost of initial workpiece
consumables: tools, cutting fluids, disposable fixtures

Some costs depend on process parameters (mainly cutting speed)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text: Tool wear

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Tool wear
Tools are subject to wear. It can affect two parts of the tool:

the flank: it changes the geometry of the tool where it contacts the workpiece, so it progressively affects surface quality and dimensional accuracy
the rake face: it changes the geometry where the tool contacts the chip: it has no effect on the workpiece, but in the long run it weakens the tool and causes it to break

If the tool and the cutting parameters are chosen correctly, flank wear occurs before rake face wear
The wear law was formulated by Taylor: \(VT^n=K\), where:

\(V\) is the cutting speed
\(T\) is the tool life
\(n\) and \(K\) are material constants; \(K\) also depends on the end-of-life criterion (application specific)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Taylor’s law
\(VT^n=K \rightarrow \log(V) - n\log(T) = \log(K) \rightarrow \log(T) = \frac{1}{n}\log(V) - \frac{1}{n}\log(K)\)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Productivity optimization
The costs of machining production are related to:

investments and overhead (fixed)
labor and raw materials (variable)
cost per piece (variable)

Costs are dependent variables. The process parameters are independent parameters






Important


We can ask whether there are process conditions that maximize productivity and/or minimize costs

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Productivity optimization — Turning





Symbol
Meaning




\(C_p\)
Cost per piece


\(C_m\)
Machining cost


\(C_s\)
Setup cost


\(C_l\)
Loading cost


\(C_t\)
Tooling cost


\(L\)
Labor cost


\(O\)
Overhead



In turning: \[
T_m = \frac{L}{fN}=\frac{\pi LD}{fV} \\
N_p = \frac{T}{T_m} = \frac{fK^{1/n}}{\pi LDV^{1/n-1}}
\]

\[\begin{align}
C_p &= C_m + C_s + C_l + C_t \\
C_m &= T_m(L_m + O_m) \\
C_l &= T_l(L_m + O_m) \\
C_t &= \frac{1}{N_p}\left[T_c(L_m+O_m) + T_g(L_g+O_g) + D_c\right] = \frac{C_{t0}}{N_p} \\
T_p &= T_{s,l} + T_m + \frac{C_{t0}}{N_p}
\end{align}\]






Note


We have \(C_p=C_p(V)\) and \(T_p = T_p(V)\), so we can differentiate both to identify an optimal condition

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Productivity optimization — Turning


Costs: \[\begin{align}
\frac{\partial C_p}{\partial V} &= 0 \\
V_{o,c} &= \frac{K(L_m+O_m)^n}{[(1/n-1)C_{t0}]^n} \\
T_{o,c} &= (1/n -1)\frac{C_{t0}}{L_m+O_m}
\end{align}\]

Times: \[\begin{align}
\frac{\partial T_p}{\partial V} &= 0 \\
V_{o,t} &= \frac{K}{[(1/n-1)T_c]^n} \\
T_{0,t} &= (1/n -1)T_c
\end{align}\]







Note


What do we optimize? Costs or times?

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Productivity optimization — Turning



The optimal cutting speed \(V_{o,c}\) corresponds to maximum economic efficiency
However, when there are penalties for delays it may be worth producing at \(V_{o,t}\), because it is the speed that maximizes productivity
So, \(V\) shall be normally set to \(V_{o,c}\), increasing it up to (but not above) \(V_{o,t}\) if there are penalties for delays

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Limits of analytical process models
Orthogonal cutting

Orthogonal cutting rarely applies. In most real machining operations chip formation is inherently 3-D
The chip formation model is idealized. In reality:

the cutting edge is never perfectly sharp
the shear plane does not have zero thickness
deformation does not occur only on the shear plane, but also on the machined surface in contact with the cutting edge and between chip and tool

The stress and strain field cannot be computed analytically
There is no reliable thermal model that accounts for friction and plastic deformation as heat sources
The strain rates involved \(\dot\gamma\) are extreme: this makes it very difficult to identify the plastic properties of the material under similar conditions

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Limits of analytical process models
Taylor’s law

It is an empirical model, i.e., it has no physical basis but rests on observation alone, so it cannot be calibrated from measurements of material properties
It is an approximate law: more complete empirical laws exist in the form \(VT^nd^xf^y=K\), which account for other process parameters that have a much smaller influence than \(V\) but still affect tool life
It is expensive to calibrate:

the experimental procedure is necessarily slow and costly
\(n\) depends on the workpiece material and on the tool material
\(K\) depends on the end-of-life criterion, so it is user-specific (i.e., it cannot be found in tables)

Even the more complete laws do not account for factors such as lubrication and cooling

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Economic optimization

The analysis above depends on being able to express \(T_m(V)\) analytically

This is possible only for elementary operations (e.g., cylindrical turning). For more complex operations the relation can only be computed point by point by simulating the process (via CAM or CNC functions, which entails considerable time and cost)
It relies on the availability of a validated and reliable wear law
It is worthwhile only for large and very large batches (economy of scale)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1

Coordinate systems
In general, the offset must also include the tool length and radius (\(T_x\) and \(T_y\)) and possibly the angle \(\theta\) of the machine \((X, Y)\) frame with the workpiece frame:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} x_m \\ y_m \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta & O_x + T_x \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & O_y + T_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
In 3-D, you use 4x4 homogeneous transformation matrices

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Coordinate transformations


Any coordinate \(P_{wp}\) given in the workpiece reference frame \(O_{wp}\) is converted in machine coordinates \(P_m\), including tool length offset
\[
P_m = T_{wp \to m} P_{wp}; \qquad
T_{wp \to m} = \begin{bmatrix} r_{11} & r_{12} & r_{13} & d_x \\ r_{21} & r_{22} & r_{23} & d_y \\ r_{31} & r_{32} & r_{33} & d_z + l_t \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]
\(d_{x-z}\) are coordinates of \(O_{wp}\) in \(O_m\)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Coordinate transformations
Remember that the roto-translation matrix is:
\[
T = \begin{bmatrix}
\cos\alpha\cos\beta & \cos\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma - \sin\alpha\cos\beta & \cos\alpha\sin\beta\cos\gamma + \sin\alpha\sin\gamma & d_x \\
\sin\alpha\cos\beta & \sin\alpha\sin\beta\sin\gamma + \cos\alpha\cos\beta & \sin\alpha\sin\beta\cos\gamma - \cos\alpha\sin\gamma & d_y \\
-\sin\beta & \cos\beta\sin\gamma & \cos\beta\cos\gamma & d_z \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]


The order of transformations is:

Roll by \(\gamma\)
Pitch by \(\beta\)
Yaw by \(\alpha\)
Translate by \((d_x, d_y, d_z)\)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Profiling
Discrete time-base (clock)









\[
\Delta t_1 = \frac{f_m - f_s}{a}, \quad
\Delta t_2 = \frac{f_m - f_e}{d}, \quad
\Delta t_m = \frac{l}{f_m} - \Delta t_1 \frac{f_m + f_s}{2 f_m} - \Delta t_2 \frac{f_e + f_m}{2 f_m}
\]
\[
\Delta t^* = \mathrm{int}\left(\frac{\Delta t}{t_q} + 1\right) t_q = \Delta t_1 + \Delta t_m^* + \Delta t_2, \qquad
\Delta t_m^* = \Delta t_m + \Delta t^* - \Delta t
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Profiling
Discrete time-base (clock)









\[
\int_{t_s}^{t_e} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \frac{\Delta t_1}{2}(f_m^* + f_s) + \Delta t_m^* f_m^* + \frac{\Delta t_2}{2}(f_m^* + f_e) = l
\]
\[
f_m^* = \frac{2l - f_s \Delta t_1 - f_e \Delta t_2}{\Delta t_1 + \Delta t_2 + 2\Delta t_m^*}, \qquad
a^* = \frac{f_m^* - f_s}{\Delta t_1}, \qquad
d^* = \frac{f_e - f_m^*}{\Delta t_2}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Profiling
Short segments, \(\Delta t_m \le 0\)












\[
\int_{t_s}^{t_e} f(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \frac{a\Delta t_1^2 + d\Delta t_2^2}{2}; \quad a\Delta t_1 = d\Delta t_2
\]
\[
\frac{\Delta t_1^2 (a + a^2/d)}{2} = l
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta t_1 &= \sqrt{\frac{2l}{a + a^2/d}} \\
\Delta t_2 &= \frac{a}{d}\Delta t_1 \\
\Delta t_2^* &= \Delta t^* - \Delta t_1
\end{aligned}
\qquad
f_m^*(\Delta t_1 + \Delta t_2^*) = 2l
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
a^* &= \frac{f_m^* - f_s}{\Delta t_1} \\
d^* &= \frac{f_e - f_m^*}{\Delta t_2^*}
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Motion interpolation



The speed profile is evaluated and integrated at each time tick
The axes set-points are calculated with the parametric equation of the path
For a linear motion:

\[
\begin{aligned}
X(t) &= X_0 + \Delta X \lambda(t) \\
Y(t) &= Y_0 + \Delta Y \lambda(t) \\
Z(t) &= Z_0 + \Delta Z \lambda(t)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Motion interpolation


For arc interpolation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
X(t) &= X_c + R\cos(\vartheta_0 + \Delta\vartheta \lambda(t)) \\
Y(t) &= Y_c + R\sin(\vartheta_0 + \Delta\vartheta \lambda(t)) \\
Z(t) &= Z_0 + \Delta Z \lambda(t)
\end{aligned}
\]
Warning: feedrate may be reduced
\[
f_{m,a} = \min\left(f_m, \sqrt{aR}\right)
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Motion interpolation
G-code syntax:

G[02|03] X[\(X_f\)] Y[\(Y_f\)] I[\(I\)] J[\(J\)]
G[02|03] X[\(X_f\)] Y[\(Y_f\)] R[\(\pm R\)]









\[
\begin{aligned}
\vartheta_0 &= \cos^{-1} I/R \\
\vartheta_f &= \cos^{-1} (X_f - X_c)/R \\
X_c &= X_0 + I \\
Y_c &= Y_0 + J \\
R &= \sqrt{I^2 + J^2} \\
R^2 &= (X_f - X_c)^2 + (Y_f - Y_c)^2
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Motion interpolation
Center coordinates (two alternatives depending on the sign of \(R\))
\[
\Delta x = X_f - X_0, \qquad \Delta y = Y_f - Y_0
\]
\[
X_c = X_0 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\Delta x - \mathrm{sign}(R)\,\frac{\sqrt{-\Delta y^2 (\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)(-4R^2 + \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)}}{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}\right)
\]
\[
Y_c = Y_0 + \frac{\Delta y}{2} + \mathrm{sign}(R)\,\frac{\Delta x \sqrt{-\Delta y^2 (\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)(-4R^2 + \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2)}}{2\Delta x^2 \Delta y + 2\Delta y^3}
\]

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Look-ahead feedrate profile

Problem 1: tangent or semi-tangent blocks shall have non-zero speed at the corner.
Problem 2: it shall be possible to accelerate to nominal feedrate with continuous acceleration over \(n\) short segments, and it may take more than one segment to decelerate down to stop

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Look-ahead feedrate profile
Approach:

Calculate \(v_i\), \(v_m\), \(v_f\) for each block, considering \(v = v(s)\)
Forward step: from block 1 to block \(n\), calculate accelerations only
Backward step: from block \(n\) to block 1, calculate decelerations only and compose with accelerations
Change variable \(s \to t\) and get \(v = v(t)\)
Reshape \(v^* = \dfrac{v(t)}{k}\), where \(k = t_f / t_f^*\) and \(t_f^*\) is the multiple of \(t_q\) immediately larger than the total time \(t_f\) (block by block)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Constant Acc/Dec

We cannot calculate feed profiles in time abscissa, for we don’t know the duration of each step
Thus we start planning in curvilinear abscissa \(s\):

\(s(t) = s_0 + v_0 t + a t^2/2\), and thus \(t(s) = \dfrac{1}{a}\left(-v_0 \pm \sqrt{2a(s - s_0) + v_0^2}\right)\)
Since \(v(t(s)) = v_0 + a\, t(s)\), it follows that \(v(s) = \sqrt{2a(s - s_0) + v_0^2}\)
So accelerations and decelerations follow a square root law of \(s\)

In jerk-limited approach, we’d have a cubic root branch at the beginning and at the end of each acc/dec branch

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Look-ahead feedrate


Step 1: calculate velocities:

\(v_{i,i} = v_{f,i-1}\), or 0 for first sg.
\(v_{m,i} = f_i\) for G01
\(v_m = \min(f_i, \sqrt{aR})\) for G02/G03
\(v_{f,i} = \dfrac{v_{m,i} + v_{m,i+1}}{2}\cos\alpha_i\)
\(v_{f,i} = 0\) for last segment or if \(v_{m,i} = 0\)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Reshape for discrete time

Calculate \(t_f^* = \lceil t_f / t_q + 1 \rceil t_q\)
Calculate \(k = t_f^* / t_f\)
Rescale feedrate so that \(v^*(t) = \dfrac{v(t)}{k}\)

title: Digital Manufacturing – Part 1
text:
Receding horizon

This algorithm requires a sequence of blocks starting and ending at zero feedrate
You can assume that G00 blocks mark full stops at corners
Nonetheless, a program can consist in thousands of sequential G01/G02/G03 blocks: memory problem
Solution:

At run time, pre-elaborate a buffer made of a limited number of blocks (say 100) assuming the last one stops (look-ahead buffer)
Re-calculate the moving buffer as soon as a block is done by adding a new block at the end (FIFO): start backward (dec) until no change, then forward (acc)
The buffer size depends on available memory and on computation time (must be shorter than the time needed to execute the buffer); calculations are done in parallel in a separate thread
